title: Styling Your Conditions
objective: Write conditions that read clearly and avoid redundant comparisons.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material. List-dependent if-statement patterns are covered later in the Collections chapter, after lists are introduced.

paragraphs: A condition that already produces a Boolean doesn't need to be compared to True or False again. is_ready == True is redundant — is_ready alone already says the same thing, and reads more naturally.
Put a single, simple space around comparison operators (a >= b, not a>=b) so the condition is easy to scan at a glance. Consistent spacing matters more than any one particular style choice.

When a condition needs a comment to explain what it checks, consider whether naming an intermediate variable would make the comment unnecessary — a variable named is_hot_enough often communicates more clearly than a comment next to a raw comparison.
explanation.rule: If a condition already evaluates to True or False, use it directly instead of comparing it to True or False again.

examples.title: Removing a Redundant Comparison
examples.code:
is_ready = temperature >= 1200

# Prefer this:
if is_ready:
    print("Go")

# Over this:
if is_ready == True:
    print("Go")
examples.note: Both work, but the first reads more like a plain sentence.

checks.question: is_valid is already a Boolean. Which condition is the better style?

feedback.correct: Correct — comparing a Boolean to True is redundant; use it directly.
feedback.incorrect: is_valid is already True or False, so comparing it to True again is redundant.

assignment.title: Direct Boolean Check
assignment.brief: Write announce(is_ready) that prints 'Go' if is_ready is True and 'Wait' otherwise, using is_ready directly (not ==True).
requirements: Use if is_ready: / else: directly, without comparing to True or False.
Print the correct message for each case.
assignment.starterCode:
def announce(is_ready):
    # Use is_ready directly, without comparing to True/False.
    pass

announce(True)
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    announce(True)
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))

hints: is_ready is already a Boolean — you don't need == True.
if is_ready: is enough to check that it's True.
Use else: for the False case, printing 'Wait'.
Calling announce(True) should print exactly: Go
